evidence.claim: The Patagonia–Sonoita Scenic Road joins SR 83 and part of SR 82 in an undivided drive through hilly grasslands and mountain valleys.
evidence.quote: SR 83 and a portion of SR 82 from a point north of Nogales to Sonoita are linked together as an official scenic byway.

evidence.claim: The Patagonia–Sonoita Scenic Road joins SR 83 and part of SR 82 in an undivided drive through hilly grasslands and mountain valleys.
evidence.quote: views through these hilly grasslands and mountain valleys from this undivided highway

evidence.claim: The Arizona Department of Transportation credits those views with making it the state’s second designated scenic road.
evidence.quote: So lovely are the views through these hilly grasslands and mountain valleys from this undivided highway that the “Patagonia–Sonoita Scenic Road” was the second road given this designation by the state of Arizona.

evidence.claim: The route now numbered SR 83 served Empire Ranch and mountain mines in the 1870s.
evidence.quote: In the 1870s, SR 83 became a transportation route for the renowned Empire Ranch and its cattle industry, as well as the newly discovered gold and silver mines in the Santa Rita Mountains and Empire Mountains.

evidence.claim: After the Southern Pacific Railroad arrived in 1881, it became the most direct connection to supplies at Pantano-Marsh Station.
evidence.quote: With the arrival of the Southern Pacific Railroad in 1881, SR 83 became the most direct way to reach railroad and supplies at the Pantano-Marsh Station

evidence.claim: Pima and Santa Cruz counties graded their sections in 1920; the state graveled the full road in 1926.
evidence.quote: In 1920, each county graded and engineered their respective segments for better drainage. In 1926, the state graveled its full length.

evidence.claim: Paving followed between 1953 and 1959, turning the old transport route into a surfaced highway.
evidence.quote: SR 83 received its first surface paving using different combinations of aggregate and binders between 1953 and 1959.

evidence.claim: SR 82 developed from paths and wagon roads carrying cattle, military supplies, ore and stagecoaches between 1854 and 1882.
evidence.quote: Foot paths, animal trails, and wagon roads associated with the movement of cattle, military personnel and supplies, silver and lead ore, and stagecoaches, as well as railroad construction, during the 1854–1882 time period established the route what would be SR 82.

evidence.claim: It remained a lightly improved dirt road until 1935; most of its 66 miles received gravel and sealant between 1938 and 1946, largely with Works Progress Administration funding.
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, SR 82 remained a dirt road with only slight improvements by grading and for drainage from 1926 until 1935.

evidence.claim: It remained a lightly improved dirt road until 1935; most of its 66 miles received gravel and sealant between 1938 and 1946, largely with Works Progress Administration funding.
evidence.quote: Not until the period between 1938 and 1946 did the vast remainder of the 66-mile road receive it first coating of mixed gravel and sealant, with funds largely provided by the federal government through the Works Progress Administration (WPA).

evidence.quote: The town is located in the valley of Sonoita Creek between the Santa Rita Mountains to the north and the Patagonia Mountains to the south. State Route 82 passes through the town. Nogales lies to the southwest and Sonoita to the northeast.

evidence.claim: Sonoita sits where SR 83 and SR 82 meet, with the headwaters of Sonoita Creek just west of town.
evidence.quote: The community is at the intersection of Arizona State Route 83 and Arizona State Route 82.

evidence.claim: Sonoita sits where SR 83 and SR 82 meet, with the headwaters of Sonoita Creek just west of town.
evidence.quote: The headwaters of Sonoita Creek are just west of the site.

evidence.claim: The Santa Rita Mountains lie to the west and the Canelo Hills to the southwest.
evidence.quote: The Santa Rita Mountains and the Canelo Hills lie to the west and southwest respectively.

evidence.claim: The road now called SR 83 carried ranching and mining traffic in the 1870s, then connected the area to the Southern Pacific Railroad at Pantano-Marsh Station after 1881.
evidence.quote: In the 1870s, SR 83 became a transportation route for the renowned Empire Ranch and its cattle industry, as well as the newly discovered gold and silver mines in the Santa Rita Mountains and Empire Mountains.

evidence.claim: The road now called SR 83 carried ranching and mining traffic in the 1870s, then connected the area to the Southern Pacific Railroad at Pantano-Marsh Station after 1881.
evidence.quote: With the arrival of the Southern Pacific Railroad in 1881, SR 83 became the most direct way to reach railroad and supplies at the Pantano-Marsh Station

evidence.claim: Its first paving came between 1953 and 1959, decades after those freight journeys.
evidence.quote: SR 83 received its first surface paving using different combinations of aggregate and binders between 1953 and 1959.

evidence.claim: Sonoita comes from the O’odham Ṣon ʼOidag, which may be best translated as “spring field”.
evidence.quote: The origin of the name of the CDP is the O'odham Ṣon ʼOidag, which may be best translated as "spring field".

evidence.claim: Patagonia occupies the Sonoita Creek valley between two mountain ranges, with SR 82 passing through town.
evidence.quote: The town is located in the valley of Sonoita Creek between the Santa Rita Mountains to the north and the Patagonia Mountains to the south. State Route 82 passes through the town.

evidence.claim: It developed as a supply and trading center for mines and ranches in the mid-19th century.
evidence.quote: It developed in the mid-19th century as a trading and supply center for nearby mines and ranches.

evidence.claim: The New Mexico and Arizona Railroad gave miners and ranchers a way to ship products out and bring manufactured goods in.
evidence.quote: The arrival of the New Mexico and Arizona Railroad to Patagonia gave the ranchers and miners a new outlet for their products and access to manufactured goods.

evidence.claim: A two-story depot was built in 1900; the railroad was abandoned in 1962.
evidence.quote:
Patagonia was recognized as the official name of the town in 1900 by the United States Postal Office Department in Washington, D.C.
That same year, a two-story railroad depot was built

evidence.claim: A two-story depot was built in 1900; the railroad was abandoned in 1962.
evidence.quote: The railroad was abandoned in 1962.

evidence.claim: The town is now an arts and crafts center as well as a tourist destination.
evidence.quote: In the 21st century, it is a tourist destination, retirement community, and arts and crafts center.

evidence.claim: The creek valley places the Santa Rita Mountains north of town and the Patagonia Mountains to its south.
evidence.quote: The town is located in the valley of Sonoita Creek between the Santa Rita Mountains to the north and the Patagonia Mountains to the south.

evidence.claim: Nogales takes its name from the walnut trees of the mountain pass between the Arizona city and its Sonoran neighbor.
evidence.quote: The town is named for the black walnut trees which once grew abundantly in the mountain pass between the cities of Nogales, Arizona, and Nogales, Sonora

evidence.claim: In 1880, Isaac and Jacob Isaacson established a trading post here; the post office first used their surname, then changed to Nogales in 1883.
evidence.quote: In 1880, Russian-Jewish immigrants Isaac and Jacob Isaacson homesteaded the trading post of Isaacson, Arizona, at present-day Nogales. The U.S. Postal Service opened the Isaacson post office but renamed it as Nogales in 1883.

evidence.claim: Cross-border trade remains central to the city’s economy.
evidence.quote: The economy of Nogales is heavily dependent on the cross-border trade through its Ports of Entry

evidence.claim: Union Pacific provides rail transportation north to Tucson on what was formerly the Southern Pacific Railroad.
evidence.quote: Rail transportation is provided by the Union Pacific Railroad (formerly the Southern Pacific Railroad) north to Tucson.

evidence.claim: On the Santa Cruz County Historical Courthouse at Morley and Court streets, the figure of Lady Justice has an unusual detail: she wears no blindfold.
evidence.quote: The Santa Cruz County Historical Courthouse on Morley Street/Court Street has the statue of Lady Justice on top of the building. The Nogales version of Lady Justice is not wearing a blindfold.

flags: The corridor-management-plan cache (14.txt) contains only a Wayback wrapper, not the plan. Telles Grotto Shrine has no usable evidence anywhere in this road’s cache and is omitted.
ADOT describes the designated corridor as ending north of Nogales; Nogales is presented as the onward town, not as an exact designation boundary.
The cache supports broad terrain and road improvements, but not travel time, the cited pass elevation or detailed grades and curves.

The Welsh-miner naming account is attributed to German Quiroga in the cache and is supportable only with that attribution; it is omitted for narrative focus. No claim is made that the depot survives or that its site is open.
